title: E-Signature Tools for Freelancers — Jon Martin
description: QuickSigner, PandaDoc, and Dropbox Sign compared for freelancers: free options, paid prices, trials, and whether your clients need an account to sign.
dek: Three ways for a freelancer or solo consultant to get contracts and statements of work signed online, without printing or chasing scans.
Prices and features below come from each vendor's own pages, checked on the date shown.

blocks.html: This is for a freelancer, contractor, or one-person consultancy that sends a few contracts a month and wants them signed quickly, with a clean record of who signed what and when.
At this size, the questions are narrow. How many documents can you send for free? What does the first paid plan cost? Do your clients have to create an account to sign?

If you send a handful of documents a month, start on a free plan; QuickSigner and PandaDoc both have one. If you send more, QuickSigner's Business plan is the cheapest paid option here. Pick PandaDoc if you also build proposals and want them in the same tool. Pick Dropbox Sign if you want unlimited signature requests and a long trial before paying.
On monthly billing, a year of QuickSigner Business comes to {{calc:quicksigner_year_monthly}} per user; paying yearly brings it to $48.

QuickSigner's Free plan is {{fact:quicksigner.free}}. Business is {{fact:quicksigner.business}}, and Professional is {{fact:quicksigner.professional}}. Template limits: {{fact:quicksigner.templates}}. There's {{fact:quicksigner.trial}}.
For clients, the key line is that {{fact:quicksigner.signers}}. That keeps the signing step to a link and a click.
PandaDoc has {{fact:pandadoc.free}}. Starter is {{fact:pandadoc.starter}}. Business is {{fact:pandadoc.business}}. There's {{fact:pandadoc.trial}}, and {{fact:pandadoc.annual}}.
One thing to know before you automate: {{fact:pandadoc.credits}}. If you plan to send documents from a {{link:zapier}} flow or from {{link:hubspot}}, read how many credits your plan includes.
Dropbox Sign Essentials is {{fact:dropbox-sign.essentials}}. Standard is {{fact:dropbox-sign.standard}}. It offers {{fact:dropbox-sign.unlimited}} and {{fact:dropbox-sign.trial}}.
On cost to clients, Dropbox Sign says {{fact:dropbox-sign.signers}}. It lists {{fact:dropbox-sign.integrations}}.

Count last quarter's contracts. If the number fits under a free plan's monthly limit, there's no reason to pay yet. If it doesn't, compare the paid plans on a yearly basis, since that's how most of them price their best rate.

Then think about what comes before the signature. If you already write proposals in a document editor and only need signing, a lean tool is enough. If the proposal itself is where you win the work, a tool that builds it and collects the signature saves a step.
Last, send yourself a test document from each tool and sign it on your phone. That's where your client will see it.
Save a signed copy to the same folder every time, named by client and date. The tool's audit trail is useful, but you want your own copy if you ever switch tools.
Use one template per service you sell, so scope and payment terms don't drift from client to client.
